segments.body: The historical sloop is a useful conceptual ancestor: a hull that can be adapted among fighting, minelaying, and minesweeping roles. That flexibility fits a constrained maritime theatre where mines and short-range operations matter greatly. It also explains why class labels matter less than mission adaptability.

evidence.note: Answer recommends submarines, corvettes, minesweepers, and adaptable sloop-type roles.

segments.summary: For the Baltic, submarines and adaptable corvette or sloop-sized vessels can fight, lay mines, or clear mines.
segments.question: Which warships are most effective in the Baltic?
segments.answerShort: Submarines plus adaptable corvette or sloop-sized ships, with minelaying and minesweeping capacity, best fit the Baltic problem.

segments.title: Economic shocks and the struggle to retain fleets
segments.body: A financial shock would make military budgets politically difficult, while continued Chinese naval growth could eventually force a response. Retaining capability and active programmes is cheaper than allowing them to collapse and trying to rebuild later. Stop-start defence policy creates substantial long-term costs.

evidence.note: Answer contrasts immediate budget pressure with the later cost of rebuilding lost capability.

segments.summary: Economic disruption makes Western fleet funding harder, but cutting established capability may cost more than maintaining programmes until conditions improve.
segments.question: How will an economic shock affect fleets over the next five years?
segments.answerShort: Funding will become harder, but maintaining programmes is usually cheaper than cutting them and rebuilding capability later.

segments.title: Balancing stealth and electronic warfare in the Baltic
segments.body: Ship stealth becomes a one-trick answer when designers rely on it alone. A Baltic combatant still benefits from lowering signatures in crowded littoral waters, combined with a stronger electronic-countermeasures suite. The mixed approach lets the ship complicate detection while also deceiving, disrupting, or degrading the systems trying to target it.

evidence.note: Answer favours a little stealth combined with extensive electronic countermeasures for a Baltic corvette.

segments.summary: A Baltic corvette benefits from reduced signatures, but electronic countermeasures offer more flexibility than treating stealth as the whole defensive system.
segments.question: Should a Baltic corvette prioritise stealth?
segments.answerShort: Use some stealth, but pair it with substantial electronic countermeasures rather than relying on low observability alone.

segments.title: Modern shipping's convoy shock
segments.body: Modern merchant shipping would face severe disruption if it suddenly had to operate under a serious convoy system. Just-in-time logistics leaves little margin for delay or the advance planning that protected shipping in earlier wars. A later exchange points to the difficulties Britain encountered while escorting flagged and friendly shipping through the Strait of Hormuz as a limited warning of the coordination problem. The issue is therefore as much economic and institutional as it is naval.

evidence.note: Answer describes panic and just-in-time logistics problems under a renewed convoy system.
Follow-up cites recent escort difficulties around the Strait of Hormuz as a warning.

segments.summary: A major naval war would collide with just-in-time logistics and commercial shipping practices that are poorly prepared for the return of convoy control.
segments.question: How would modern shipping companies react to a major naval war?
segments.answerShort: They would face a severe shock: just-in-time supply chains and present practices are poorly prepared for large-scale convoy control.

segments.title: How warships protect against chemical and biological contamination
segments.body: Salt water, wind, and weather complicate the effective use of mustard gas against ships. Modern warships nevertheless retain chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear protection measures. They can seal internal spaces and wet or wash down exposed surfaces to remove contaminants. Maritime CBRN defence depends on whole-ship systems and environmental conditions rather than armour alone.

evidence.note: Answer discusses maritime limits on mustard gas and ship sealing and washdown systems for CBRN defence.

segments.summary: Warships use sealed spaces and washdown systems to remove contamination, while sea weather makes persistent mustard-gas attack less straightforward.
segments.question: Do warships have chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear protection?
segments.answerShort: Yes. Ships can seal themselves and use washdown systems to clear chemical or biological contamination from exposed surfaces.

segments.title: A rotary UAV is more plausible than a helicopter-carrier submarine
segments.body: A helicopter-carrier submarine is unattractive, although a submarine-launched rotary-wing uncrewed aircraft remains plausible. The distinction moves the problem from supporting a crewed aviation detachment to deploying a much smaller remote sensor or vehicle. The idea remains speculative, but it identifies a narrower mission that fits submarine constraints more plausibly.

evidence.note: Answer dismisses a helicopter-carrier submarine but suggests a rotary uncrewed aircraft as a narrower possibility.

segments.summary: The crewed helicopter-carrier submarine is dismissed, but a submarine-launched rotary uncrewed aircraft is retained as a more credible route to limited airborne sensing.
segments.question: Is a helicopter-carrier submarine a useful idea?
segments.answerShort: Not as a crewed helicopter carrier, though launching a compact rotary uncrewed aircraft could be worth exploring.

segments.title: Countering mobile shore-based anti-ship missiles
segments.body: The compact answer focuses on the targeting system rather than only the missile itself. A naval force must disrupt the sensors, communications, and targeting links that allow a mobile launcher to engage, while also seeking the launcher directly. This is the core operational problem of fighting inside a modern missile threat zone.

evidence.note: Answer identifies attacking the kill chain or launcher as the central response.

segments.summary: The basic response to mobile coastal anti-ship missiles is to find and break the kill chain, or destroy the launchers before they can fire.
segments.question: How do modern navies deal with mobile shore-based anti-ship missiles?
segments.answerShort: They try to find and disrupt the kill chain or destroy the launcher before it can fire.
